entry: 15th-century [[Inca Empire|Inca]] citadel in the Eastern Cordillera of southern [[Peru]]. Perched at 2,430 m (7,970 ft) above the Urubamba River, about 80 km (50 miles) northwest of [[Cusco]], it is believed to have been an estate of the emperor [[Pachacuti]], though no contemporary records confirm this. Radiocarbon dating places its occupation between c. 1420 and 1530, and the site was likely abandoned during the Spanish conquest. Its dry-stone walls follow the classical Inca style. The site was brought to international attention in 1911 by the American historian Hiram Bingham III. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983, it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007, and as of 2025 it receives over 1.5 million visitors a year.

River in northern Canada, the longest river system in the country. Its main stem flows 1,738 km (1,080 mi) north-northwest from [[Great Slave Lake]] to the [[Arctic Ocean]], where it forms a large delta. With its tributaries, the system is 4,241 km (2,635 mi) long, the 13th longest on Earth. The river runs entirely within the [[Northwest Territories]], though its tributaries reach five other Canadian provinces and territories. Its ultimate source is Thutade Lake in [[British Columbia]]. Inuvialuit and Gwich'in peoples lived along the river for thousands of years, and it later provided the main route into Canada's northern interior for European explorers. Oil discovered at Norman Wells in the 1920s began industrialization of the valley. Metallic minerals found in the basin include uranium, gold, lead and zinc.

Common name for pelagic fish, mostly of the family Scombridae. Mackerel are found in temperate and tropical seas, typically in the open ocean. They typically have deeply forked tails and vertical, tiger-like stripes on their backs. Many stocks migrate along coasts in large [[Shoal|schools]] to spawn in shallow water. Smaller mackerel are forage fish for larger predators, including Atlantic cod, and seabirds, [[Whale|whales]], dolphins, [[Shark|sharks]], [[Tuna]] and [[Marlin]] follow their schools. Mackerel flesh is high in omega-3 oils, and over 5 million tons were landed by commercial fishermen in 2009. Sport fishermen value the fighting ability of the king mackerel.

Small deciduous tree or large shrub of the mulberry family, [[Moraceae]], native to the south-central United States. Known as Osage orange or hedge apple, *Maclura pomifera* typically grows 8 to 15 m (30–50 ft) tall. Its bumpy, yellow-green fruit resembles an orange but is unrelated to it, and its sticky latex and woody pulp mean it is not usually eaten by humans. Settlers planted the thorny trees as hedges to exclude [[Livestock|free-range livestock]] from gardens and fields until barbed wire was invented in 1874. The Osage Nation prized its wood for bows, and early French settlers called the tree *bois d'arc* ("bow-wood").

Australian media franchise of post-apocalyptic [[Action film|action films]], created by George Miller and Byron Kennedy. It began with *Mad Max* (1979) and includes *Mad Max 2* (1981; *The Road Warrior* in the United States), *Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome* (1985) and *Mad Max: Fury Road* (2015). Miller directed all four films. [[Mel Gibson]] originally played the title character, Max Rockatansky, and [[Tom Hardy]] took over in the later films. *Fury Road* won six of its ten Academy Award nominations in 2016, the first franchise film to receive such recognition. The series has had a highly positive reception and significantly influenced post-apocalyptic fiction.

American period drama television series, broadcast on AMC from 2007 to 2015. Created by Matthew Weiner, *Mad Men* ran for seven seasons and 92 episodes. It follows Don Draper (Jon Hamm), a creative director at Sterling Cooper, a [[Manhattan]] advertising agency, from March 1960 to November 1970. Critics praised its writing, acting and historical authenticity. The series won 16 Emmy Awards. It was the first basic cable series to win the Emmy for Outstanding Drama Series, doing so in each of its first four seasons. It is widely regarded as a key series of the Golden Age of Television.

Island country in the Indian Ocean, off the southeastern coast of Africa. Madagascar is the world's fourth-largest island and the second-largest island country. Its capital and largest city is [[Antananarivo]]. The island split from Africa about 180 million years ago, and its isolation produced a biodiversity hotspot in which over 90% of wildlife is endemic. Austronesian peoples first settled it by the mid-first millennium CE, and Bantu groups followed around the ninth century. Merina nobles united most of the island as the Kingdom of Madagascar in the early 19th century. The monarchy ended in 1897 with France's annexation, and the country gained independence in 1960. After mass protests in 2025, a military coup installed Michael Randrianirina as president. Madagascar is a member of the [[United Nations]] and the [[African Union]], and remains a least-developed country.

Novel by French writer [[Gustave Flaubert]], published in 1856 and 1857. Flaubert's debut novel was serialized in *Revue de Paris* from October to December 1856. Its title character, Emma Bovary, lives beyond her means to escape the tedium of provincial life. Prosecutors called the novel obscene, and the trial of January 1857 made it notorious. Flaubert was acquitted on February 7, 1857. *Madame Bovary* became a bestseller when it was published in two volumes in April 1857. A seminal work of literary realism, it is ranked among Flaubert's masterpieces and as one of the most influential literary works in history.

Autonomous region of Portugal, an archipelago in the North Atlantic Ocean about 805 km (500 miles) southwest of mainland [[Portugal]]. It lies just under 400 km (250 mi) north of the [[Canary Islands]] and is an outermost region of the [[European Union]]. Its population was 251,060 in 2021, and roughly half of it lives in Funchal, the capital on the main island's south coast. Portuguese sailors in the service of [[Prince Henry the Navigator]] claimed the uninhabited islands in 1419, and settlement followed after 1420. The archipelago was the first territorial discovery of the [[Age of Discovery]]. In the late 15th century it exported slave-cultivated sugar, and in the 18th century, wine. Tourism is now central, and the pre-historic laurel forest is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Major South American waterway and the largest tributary of the [[Amazon River]]. Estimated at 1,450 km (900 mi) long, the Madeira accounts for about 15% of the water in the Amazon basin. Just below its confluence, its mean inter-annual discharge is 18,000 cubic metres per second, approximately half that of the [[Congo River]]. Its tributaries drain the northeastern slopes of the [[Andes]] and part of Brazil's Mato Grosso. From its source at the confluence of the Madre de Dios and Mamoré rivers, it flows north along the border between [[Bolivia]] and [[Brazil]]. Its falls near Porto Velho, once a barrier to navigation, are now submerged by the reservoir of the Santo Antônio Dam.

Indian actress and film producer, a leading star of the Golden Age of Hindi cinema. Born Mumtaz Jehan Begum Dehlavi in [[Delhi]], she moved as a child to Bombay (now [[Mumbai]]). She began as a child artiste in 1942 and became a leading lady after *Lal Dupatta* (1948) and the gothic film *Mahal* (1949). Her beauty earned her the nickname "Venus of the Indian screen", though later critics argued that her appeal often overshadowed her acting. Her portrayal of Anarkali in the epic *Mughal-e-Azam* (1960) has been named by critics among the finest performances in Indian cinema. Her comic roles in *Mr. & Mrs. '55* (1955) and *Gateway of India* (1957) brought renewed success. She suffered from a ventricular septal defect throughout her adult life, and her marriage to [[Kishore Kumar]] drew considerable media attention.

Indian actress and television personality. Born in [[Mumbai]], she made her acting debut in 1984 in *Abodh*. Her breakthrough came with the action drama *Tezaab* (1988), and she became established in top-grossing romantic dramas including *Dil* (1990), *Beta* (1992), *Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!* (1994) and *Dil To Pagal Hai* (1997). She won four Filmfare Awards for Best Actress for these films. In 2008 the Government of India awarded her the Padma Shri, the fourth-highest civilian honour in the country. She has worked with [[UNICEF]] since 2014 to advocate for children's rights and to prevent child labour, and she has appeared in over 70 Hindi films.

Indian philosopher and theologian, chief proponent of the [[Vedanta|Dvaita school of Vedanta]]. Born near Udupi on the west coast of [[Karnataka]], he became a monk as a teenager. He wrote commentaries on the principal [[Upanishads]], the [[Bhagavad Gita]] and the Brahma Sutras, and is credited with 37 works in Sanskrit. He taught that the individual soul and [[Brahman]], identified with God Vishnu, are two different, unchanging realities, and that liberation is achievable only through the grace of God. He criticized the non-dualist teachings of [[Adi Shankara]] and the qualified non-dualism of [[Ramanuja]]. He established the Krishna Mutt at Udupi. His school influenced [[Vaishnavism]] and the Bhakti movement in medieval India.

State in central India, with [[Bhopal]] as its capital. It is the second-largest Indian state by area and the fifth-largest by population, with over 72 million residents. Several states were reorganized in 1956 to form Madhya Pradesh, and its southeastern [[Chhattisgarh]] region became a separate state in 2000. Its economy is the 10th-largest in India. Rich in minerals, it has the largest reserves of [[Diamond|diamonds]] and [[Copper]] in India, and it leads the country in production of pulses and oilseeds.

Multi-purpose indoor arena in Midtown [[Manhattan]], [[New York City]]. The current building, the fourth venue to bear the name, opened on February 11, 1968, on the site of the old Pennsylvania Station. Earlier Gardens stood near Madison Square, which was named after [[James Madison]]. The arena is home to the New York Rangers of the [[National Hockey League]] and the New York Knicks of the [[National Basketball Association]], and it is the oldest arena in the NBA. It also hosts boxing, [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestling]], [[Mixed martial arts]], concerts and circuses.

Capital of [[Wisconsin|the U.S. state of Wisconsin]], the second-most populous city in the state. Founded in 1836, it was named after [[James Madison]]. The city is home to the Wisconsin State Capitol and to the University of Wisconsin–Madison, the flagship campus of the state university system. Its population was 269,840 at the 2020 census, and tourism generated over $1 billion in 2018. Regarded as Wisconsin's most politically liberal city, Madison has one of the highest numbers of parks and playgrounds per capita among the 100 largest U.S. cities. Nine National Historic Landmarks include several buildings designed by [[Frank Lloyd Wright]].

American singer, songwriter and actress, dubbed the "Queen of Pop". Born and raised in Michigan, she moved to New York City in 1978 to pursue a career in dance, then performed in rock bands before releasing her self-titled debut album in 1983. Her works address social, political, sexual and religious themes, and she is known for continual reinvention. Her albums include *Like a Virgin* (1984), *True Blue* (1986) and *The Immaculate Collection* (1990). She is the best-selling female music artist of all time and the first female performer to accumulate US$1 billion from her concerts. She won a Golden Globe Award for her portrayal of [[Eva Perón]] in *Evita* (1996), and she was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in her first year of eligibility.

Capital and largest city of [[Spain]], on the River Manzanares in the central [[Iberian Peninsula]]. Madrid had over 3.4 million residents in the city proper in 2025, and about 6.8 million in its metropolitan area. It is the second-largest city in the [[European Union]], after Berlin. The site was a walled military outpost under the Emirate of Córdoba before Christian conquest in 1083 or 1085. From 1561 it was the permanent seat of the royal court, which fostered its role as an administrative center. The metropolitan area concentrates the bulk of Spain's banking operations and hosts major companies such as Telefónica, Iberia and BBVA. The Prado Museum and Reina Sofía Museum are part of the [[UNESCO]] World Heritage "Golden Triangle of Art" along the Paseo del Prado.

City in the Indian state of [[Tamil Nadu]], one of the oldest cities in India and South Asia. Located on the Vaigai River, Madurai has a documented history of more than 2,500 years and is called the cultural capital of Tamil Nadu. It was ruled in turn by the Pandyan Kingdom, the Chola Empire, the Madurai Sultanate, the Vijayanagar Empire and the Madurai Nayaks. Its population was 1,470,755 in 2011, making it the third-largest metropolis in the state after [[Chennai]] and [[Coimbatore]]. The Meenakshi Temple is one of its most prominent monuments. The city has automobile, rubber, chemical and [[Granite|granite]] manufacturing industries.

American actress, singer, comedian and playwright, and a prominent sex symbol of her time. West began performing in vaudeville as a child and moved from the New York stage to films in [[Los Angeles]]. By 1933 she was one of the largest box-office draws in the United States, and by 1935 the highest-paid woman in the country. Her sexually confident characters and double entendres repeatedly clashed with censors, and in 1938 she was included in the "Box Office Poison" list. Her films include *She Done Him Wrong* and *I'm No Angel* (both 1933), *Belle of the Nineties* (1934) and *My Little Chickadee* (1940). She later wrote books and plays and performed in [[Las Vegas]] and London. West received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

Ancient region and kingdom in eastern India, based in the [[Ganges]] Plain and one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas. Its initial territory corresponded to the modern Patna and Gaya districts of [[Bihar]]. Several dynasties ruled it and overshadowed or conquered the other Mahajanapadas. Magadha formed the core of the Haryanka, Nanda, Mauryan, Shunga and Gupta empires. It played an important role in the development of [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]]. [[Mahavira]] and [[The Buddha|the Buddha]] were contemporaries of its early rulers, Bimbisara and Ajatashatru. [[Chandragupta Maurya]] overthrew the Nanda dynasty and founded the [[Maurya Empire]].

Periodical publication, print or digital, produced at regular intervals and containing a variety of textual and visual content. Magazines are generally financed by [[Advertising|advertising]], purchase price, prepaid subscriptions or a combination of these. They are categorized by frequency, such as weekly, monthly or quarterly, by target audience and by subject. Unlike [[Newspaper|newspapers]], they are published less often and emphasize feature content for specialized audiences. The modern magazine emerged in 17th-century Europe. The first true example, *Erbauliche Monaths-Unterredungen*, was launched in Germany by theologian Johann Rist between 1663 and 1668. Many print magazines have since moved wholly or partly online, through [[Website|websites]] and digital editions. The word derives from the Arabic *makhāzin*, meaning depot or storehouse.

Main river of [[Colombia]], flowing north through the western half of the country. It takes its name from [[Mary Magdalene]]. The river flows about 1,528 km (949 mi) from the [[Andes]] to the Caribbean Sea and is navigable through much of its lower reaches, as far as Honda. Its [[Drainage basin|drainage basin]] covers 273,000 square kilometres (105,000 sq mi), about 24% of the country's area, where 66% of its population lives. The basin is rich in fish, and its annual fish harvest fell by about 90% between 1975 and 2008. The main threats are pollution and habitat loss from [[Dam|dams]]. Hippopotamuses imported by [[Pablo Escobar]] became feral after his death and are an invasive threat to the river.

16th-century Spanish maritime expedition that was the first to circumnavigate the Earth. It was planned by Portuguese explorer [[Ferdinand Magellan]] to find a western route to the Moluccas, or Spice Islands, because Portugal controlled the eastern route under the 1494 [[Treaty of Tordesillas]]. The five-ship fleet left Spain on September 20, 1519, with about 270 men. It passed through the [[Strait of Magellan]] into the Pacific, which Magellan named Mar Pacifico. Magellan was killed in battle in the Philippines in April 1521, and the Spanish navigator Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage. Only 18 men and one ship, the *Victoria*, returned to Spain in September 1522. Hardships included [[Scurvy|scurvy]], starvation and mutinies.

Purplish-pink color, located midway between blue and red on the [[RGB color model|RGB]] and [[CMYK color model|CMYK]] color wheels. It is one of the four subtractive ink colors used in most color printing, along with [[Yellow]], [[Cyan]] and black. Magenta is an extra-spectral color, as no color of the visible spectrum has its hue. The name comes from an aniline dye patented in 1859 by the French chemist François-Emmanuel Verguin, originally called fuchsine. It was renamed to celebrate the French-Sardinian victory under [[Napoleon III]] at the Battle of Magenta against the [[Austrian Empire]] that year.
